rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods - 3-year factorial field experiment (2005-2007) at Citra, FL with SMS-controlled (SUR, SDI) vs fixed-time (TIME) drip irrigation on tomato. Q2: Table 1 - irrigation applied under SMS-controlled SUR was 78/186/227 mm vs 215/391/380 mm for TIME; Fig. 3 - percolated volume consistently lower for SUR and SDI than TIME; Table 5/Fig. 4 - cumulative NO3-N leached 2-7 kg/ha for SUR/SDI vs 10-62 kg/ha for TIME; Abstract/Conclusions - SMS-based systems significantly reduced irrigation water use, percolation and nitrate leaching. Q4: Fig. 6 and Section 3.2 - capacitance probes at 0.12/0.37/0.67 m show TIME soil moisture spikes above field capacity draining to deeper layers, while SMS treatments showed minimal moisture change at depth; Fig. 3 lysimeter drainage volumes; authors state this demonstrates the mechanistic driving force of leaching. Q8: Section 2 - twin-line (separate irrigation and fertigation lines) set-up was for experimental convenience, commercial growers would use one surface line; Section 3.2 - EC readings not ion specific, other soil ions may have influenced measured EC. Q9: Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 - error bars give standard error of the mean (n=4) for cumulative leachate volume and NO3-N leaching; Table 2 reports CV%.
rows.notes: Water applied (Table 1) is measured by a single method (irrigation metering); reduced water loss below root zone is supported by both lysimeters and in-situ probes, but core water-saving result is one method, so Q3 answered no with doubt. Detailed irrigation reductions (67-216% less for SUR) are drawn from companion paper Zotarelli et al. 2009, though Table 1 in this paper reports applied volumes. Single site, single sandy soil, single crop; no requirement conditions explicitly stated beyond the sandy-soil context.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods - 3-year field experiment with SMS-controlled vs fixed-time drip irrigation on tomato. Q2: Table 3 and Section 3.1 - SMS-controlled SUR and SDI produced significantly higher shoot and fruit dry biomass than TIME (fruit dry weight 37%, 17% and 16% higher in 2005, 2006, 2007); total plant N accumulation 12-37% higher than TIME. Q4: Table 4 and Fig. 2 - petiole sap NO3 and leaf N lower in TIME, N-uptake rates lower for TIME; Section 3.1 - authors link excessive leaching under TIME to reduced crop N uptake, hampered canopy development and yield; Table 5 leaching data. Q8: Section 2 - twin-line layout due to experimental convenience unlike commercial practice; Section 3.1 - 2005 season had unfavourable hot, wet conditions and bacterial spot limiting yield. Q9: Table 2 - CV% reported for shoot and fruit biomass and N accumulation; Fig. 2 - error bars standard error (n=4) for N accumulation.
rows.notes: Fresh marketable yield (11-26% increase for SDI and SUR) is reported in the companion paper Zotarelli et al. 2009 and only cited here; this paper reports fruit and shoot dry biomass and N accumulation. Single method (plant harvest), single site/crop/soil, plot scale.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a 3-year plot experiment on one sandy soil with one tomato cultivar; irrigation volume detail and fresh yield are partly reported in a companion paper.
